deep.reconstruction:
Problem: derive Bradley's empirical refraction rule (refraction = a·tan(Z − b·refraction), Bradley's values a ≈ 57″, b ≈ 3) exactly from a physical model of the atmosphere. The model is a stratified spherical atmosphere in which the refractive index varies as a power of the distance from the Earth's centre.

(a) Snell's law in concentric layers. Gauss's M is the ratio of sines from vacuum into a layer, so M = 1/n, where n is the refractive index. I, R are the incidence angle and radius at the top of the atmosphere. The invariant is
R sin I = R' sin I'/M' = R'' sin I''/M'' = … = r sin i/m,
where i is the angle of the ray with the local radius vector at radius r. This is the modern invariant n r sin i = const.

(b) Ray geometry. Let v be the angle at the Earth's centre. Then
r dv/dr = tan i = R m sin I / sqrt(r² − R² m² sin² I).

(c) Power-law model. Put m = (r/R)^μ, i.e. n ∝ r^(−μ).
- The invariant becomes r^(1−μ) sin i = R^(1−μ) sin I.
- Taking the logarithmic differential: (1−μ) dr/r + cot i di = 0.
- Hence dv = tan i dr/r = −di/(1−μ), and v = C − i/(1−μ). The ray equation integrates in closed form.

(d) Boundary values. At the observer: i = Z (apparent zenith distance), m = 𝔐, r = 𝔑, v = 0. So C = Z/(1−μ) and i = Z − (1−μ)v. At the top v = V, so I = Z − (1−μ)V.

(e) Geometry of the total deviation. The true zenith distance is V + I = Z + ρ, where ρ is the refraction. Eliminating V gives μI = μZ − (1−μ)ρ, so I = Z − ((1−μ)/μ)ρ.
Substituting into the invariant R sin I = 𝔑 sin Z/𝔐 with 𝔐 = (𝔑/R)^μ gives
sin(Z − ((1−μ)/μ)ρ) = (𝔑/R)^(1−μ) sin Z.

(f) Normalisation. Put (1−μ)/μ = 2n, and let h be the horizontal refraction. Taking Z = 90°, ρ = h gives (𝔑/R)^(1−μ) = cos 2nh. Hence
(1) sin(Z − 2nρ) = cos 2nh · sin Z.
Forming sin Z ∓ sin(Z − 2nρ) and using 1 ∓ cos 2nh:
(2) sin nρ cos(Z − nρ) = sin² nh · sin Z
(3) cos nρ sin(Z − nρ) = cos² nh · sin Z
Dividing (2) by (3):
tan nρ = tan² nh · tan(Z − nρ).
This is exactly Bradley's form. For small angles, ρ ≈ n h² tan(Z − nρ), so b = n and a = n h². Bradley's b = 3 corresponds to n = 3, i.e. μ = 1/7. a = 57″ then gives h ≈ 33′, a realistic horizontal refraction. [These numerical identifications are mine.]

(g) Explicit solution for tan Z. Put t = tan nρ and T = tan nh. Then tan(Z − nρ) = t/T², and
tan Z = (t/T² + t)/(1 − t²/T²) = (2tT/(T² − t²)) · ((1 + T²)/(2T)).
Since (1 + T²)/(2T) = 1/sin 2nh, this is equivalent to 2tT/(T² − t²) = tan Z sin 2nh.

(h) Auxiliary-angle solution for ρ.
(4) Define y by cos Z = cos(Z − 2nρ) cos y.
- From (1), cos²(Z − 2nρ) = 1 − sin² Z cos² 2nh.
- Hence cos² Z/cos² y + sin² Z cos² 2nh = 1 = cos² Z + sin² Z.
- So cos² Z tan² y = sin² Z sin² 2nh, i.e. tan y = tan Z sin 2nh.
Half-angle forms of (4), each verified by the product formulas:
(5) cos(Z − 2nρ) sin²(y/2) = sin nρ sin(Z − nρ)
(6) cos(Z − 2nρ) cos²(y/2) = cos nρ cos(Z − nρ)
Dividing (5) by (6) gives tan²(y/2) = tan nρ tan(Z − nρ). Combining with (3)/(2), i.e. tan(Z − nρ) = tan nρ/tan² nh:
tan²(y/2) tan² nh = tan² nρ.

Result: a two-step closed-form computation of the refraction under the power-law atmosphere:
- tan y = tan Z · sin 2nh
- tan nρ = tan nh · tan(y/2)
This is consistent with (g), since 2tT/(T² − t²) = tan y when t = T tan(y/2).
errors: No mathematical errors found; every step checks.
Notation only: 'sin Z−nρ' and 'cos Z−nρ' in (5) and (6) mean sin(Z−nρ) and cos(Z−nρ). 'tang nh²' means tan²(nh), following Gauss's usual convention.
In the tan i formula the factor in the numerator should be the top-of-atmosphere radius R (as in R sin I), not fraktur 𝔑. The handwriting is ambiguous; the derivation requires R.
Gauss's M is the vacuum-to-layer ratio of sines (M = 1/n). This is unconventional but used consistently, so R sin I = R' sin I'/M' is correct as written.
The step V + I = Z + ρ uses the geometry implicitly: the true zenith distance at the observer equals the central angle plus the incidence angle at the top. This is standard and correct.

results.what: Invariant n r sin i = const for refraction in a spherically stratified atmosphere, and ray equation r dv/dr = tan i
Index law n ∝ r^(−μ) makes the ray equation integrable: v = (Z − i)/(1−μ), giving sin(Z − ((1−μ)/μ)ρ) = (𝔑/R)^(1−μ) sin Z
results.modern_name: Exactly solvable power-law refraction model (Simpson-type hypothesis)
results.usually_credited_to: Thomas Simpson (1743), whose theory yields a refraction rule of Bradley's form; discussed later by Kramp, Laplace and Bessel

results.what: Exact form tan nρ = tan² nh · tan(Z − nρ), reducing to Bradley's rule ρ = n h² tan(Z − nρ); Bradley's b = 3 corresponds to μ = 1/7
results.modern_name: Bradley's refraction formula ρ = a tan(Z − bρ)
results.usually_credited_to: James Bradley (c. 1750, published via Maskelyne 1763); theoretical basis Simpson 1743

results.what: Closed-form solution via auxiliary angle: tan y = tan Z sin 2nh, tan nρ = tan nh tan(y/2); equivalently 2tT/(T² − t²) = tan Z sin 2nh
results.modern_name: Auxiliary-angle (logarithm-friendly) explicit solution of Bradley's implicit refraction equation
results.usually_credited_to: unsure (a computational device of the period)

The added auxiliary-angle closed-form solution is elegant but elementary trigonometry. Gauss's interest in refraction theory is known, and nothing here anticipates later work.

'r^(1−μ) [−R−] sin i': Gauss struck a stray 'R' (written over 'sin'). The intended line is r^(1−μ) sin i = R^(1−μ) sin I.
In (4) the struck-through symbol before y is a corrected 'cos'; the intended relation is cos Z = cos(Z−2nρ) cos y. Likewise the next line reads cos² Z / cos² y + sin² Z cos² 2nh = 1.
'cos Z² [−cot−] tg y² = sin Z² sin 2nh²': 'cot' was struck and replaced by 'tg'. The next line reads tg y = tg Z · sin 2nh.
(5) and (6) should read cos(Z−2nρ) sin²(½y) = sin nρ sin(Z−nρ) and cos(Z−2nρ) cos²(½y) = cos nρ cos(Z−nρ).
